text:
As President Donald Trump’s approval rating falls to a historic low of 36 percent, even conservatives who supported his agenda are being forced to confront the political damage inflicted by his second administration—and the growing burden placed on ordinary people. Pollster and political analyst Cornell Belcher described the situation as “what a crater looks like in politics” and said, “By every key objective measure this is clearly a failed presidency.”

Trump’s approval rating was already weak, but the latest decline ranks among the sharpest drops of either term. The president now faces a series of crises, many stemming directly from decisions made by his own administration, while their consequences are increasingly borne by working people and economically vulnerable households.

The economy is the most immediate concern. In 2024, voters overwhelmingly ranked it as their top issue, giving it its strongest influence since the Great Recession of 2008. The cost of living surged after COVID-19. Although then-President Joe Biden’s administration reduced inflation and the economy rebounded faster than that of any other nation, financially strained voters turned to Trump because they believed his economic approach would outperform Kamala Harris, who was widely seen as a continuation of Biden.

Those expectations have not been met. Only 29 percent of Americans now approve of Trump’s handling of the economy, while just 25 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living. Republican strategist and lawyer Amanda Makki said, “It’s important that people know that the president feels their pain and that help is on the way.”

But rhetoric about recognizing hardship has not been matched by convincing action to protect working people. As economic pressure mounted under his tariffs, Trump drew criticism for remarks such as, “maybe the children will have 2 dolls instead of 30,” trivializing the sacrifices families are being forced to make.

Rising gas prices have further weakened confidence in the administration and are tied directly to the second major source of public dissatisfaction: Trump’s war on Iran. Just 35 percent of Americans approve of his actions there, down from 37 percent a week earlier. Only 26 percent agree with Trump’s claim that the war will make the United States safer, and just 7 percent support his suggestion of putting troops on the ground.

With gas prices rising to a national average just below $4 and no clear end to the conflict, Americans are increasingly concerned that the military “excursion” is imposing real costs on working families at the pump. Trump may dismiss affordability concerns as a “Democratic hoax,” but voters are not persuaded—and the administration’s policies continue to shift the costs of its failures onto people with the least power to absorb them.

rationales.valence: The narrator presents a distinctly negative appraisal of the administration, emphasizing failed expectations, economic hardship, and costs imposed on working people. The factual reporting keeps it from being maximally negative.
rationales.arousal: The language conveys moderate urgency through references to crises, sharp declines, and mounting costs, while the measured statistics and analytical delivery temper the intensity.
rationales.dominance: The narrator sounds assertive in its criticism, but conveys little personal agency or helplessness. The focus on people bearing costs with limited power concerns the people described, not clearly the narrator’s own sense of control.

ambiguities: The passage is forcefully critical, but its predominantly analytical style limits how much emotional intensity can be inferred.
The description of ordinary people as having the least power indicates their portrayed lack of agency, not necessarily the narrator’s own dominance.
